query: Consider the following context: High entropy alloy nanoparticles bring hope to developing more efficient nanomaterials for high‐temperature applications. Nevertheless, the enhanced thermal stability of nearly equiatomic nanoalloys containing at least 5 metals is nothing more than theoretical speculation about the impact of thermodynamic contributions on their structural properties and remains to be proven. In that context, which method can be used for investigate at the atomic scale the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Under high-temperature conditions, in situ aberration‐corrected (scanning) transmission electron microscopy (AC-(S)TEM) equipped with heating holders will reveal temperature‐induced atomic-scale structural changes—such as onset of atomic diffusion, local ordering variations, or phase segregation—in nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles, thereby providing direct experimental evidence of their thermal behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: Nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt high entropy alloy nanoparticles with a homogeneous, disordered solid-solution structure at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Heating the nanoparticles in situ within an AC-(S)TEM using dedicated heating holders to attain high temperature conditions.
generation.conditions: Controlled temperature ramping under TEM high-vacuum (or controlled environmental) conditions; temperatures should span from room temperature up to the range where theoretical models predict structural changes (e.g., approaching several hundred °C, though the exact threshold is uncertain).
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic lattice structure and local chemical ordering observed via high-resolution imaging and diffraction in the (S)TEM.
generation.mechanism: Thermally activated atom diffusion or local rearrangements overcome kinetic barriers, potentially triggering phase segregation or ordering transitions that alter the originally uniform high entropy structure. These changes are expected to manifest as modifications in diffraction contrast and lattice fringe patterns.
generation.predicted_outcome: Gradual changes in the atomic arrangement visible in real time: the nanoparticles will largely retain their equiatomic homogeneous structure up to a critical temperature, beyond which observable local compositional fluctuations or segregation occur.
generation.baseline: Room temperature AC-(S)TEM images showing a homogeneous atomic-scale structure without significant phase demixing.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is bounded by the temperature range applicable to high-temperature applications; if heating remains significantly below or above the regime where thermodynamic contributions lead to structural transitions, the observed behavior may not capture the predicted dynamics.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature threshold for the onset of detectable structural transitions is uncertain and may vary with nanoparticle size, strain, and local environment. In addition, the dominant mode of structural evolution (e.g., gradual diffusion vs. sudden phase segregation) is not pre-determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles and mount them in an AC-(S)TEM equipped with a temperature-controlled heating holder. Increment the temperature in defined steps while continuously imaging the atomic structure and recording diffraction patterns. Compare real-time images at each temperature step to detect any changes in atomic ordering or the emergence of secondary phases.
measurements: High-resolution lattice imaging to detect atomic-scale ordering and structural integrity
Selected area electron diffraction patterns to identify changes in phase composition
Time-resolved image series to monitor the kinetics of any observed transformations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, upon increasing the temperature over the expected relevant range, there is no measurable change in the atomic lattice images or diffraction patterns (i.e., the nanoparticles maintain a homogeneous structure without any detectable local ordering or phase segregation), then the hypothesis that thermally activated structural changes occur under these conditions is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

A second prominent class of HEA systems are refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), which comprise mostly refractory elements and invariably crystallize as body-centered cubic ( bcc ) solid solutions; these alloys have been considered as promising candidate materials for elevated-temperature applications due to their exceptional resistance to softening and extremely high melting points [9] – [11] .
